title: Causal Inference, Experiments & Confounding
excerpt: Causal inference asks what would have happened to the same people, places or firms under a different policy or treatment. Compare experiments and observational designs, use counterfactual reasoning, and identify the assumptions needed before a difference between groups can be called an effect.
objectives: Explain why association and prediction alone cannot identify a causal effect.
Define counterfactuals, treatment effects and estimands in clear financial examples.
Use random assignment, DAGs and adjustment rules to reason about confounding, mediators and colliders.
Evaluate difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity and instrumental-variable designs through their assumptions.
Separate identification, uncertainty, statistical evidence, practical importance and generalization.

lessons.title: Association is not the missing counterfactual
lessons.body:
A causal question asks what would happen to the same unit under two alternatives, such as receiving a budgeting message versus not receiving it. We can observe only one of those potential outcomes for each customer; the unobserved outcome is the counterfactual. A difference in average returns or enrollment is an association until a design makes the comparison credible. Confounding, reverse causality, selection and chance can all create a pattern. Random sampling mainly supports generalization to a population; random assignment mainly supports comparable treatment groups. Define the unit, treatment, outcome, time window and target population before calculating an effect in context.

A useful way to see the problem is to imagine a job-training programme. In an illustrative record, people who attended later earn £25,000 on average and people who did not attend earn £22,000, a raw gap of £3,000. That is a real difference between the observed groups, but it is not yet the programme effect. People who chose training may already have had more time, support or motivation. For each trainee, the key missing comparison is what that same person would have earned at the same time without training.

Causal inference defines the target first—for example, the average effect of offering training to eligible jobseekers—then asks which design can estimate the missing alternative. Random assignment, a policy threshold or a defensible comparison over time can help, but each relies on different assumptions and may answer a different population-level question. A regression adjustment cannot prove those assumptions just by including many variables. The Penn State notes on bias and confounding and the World Bank DIME causal-inference materials linked below give more examples.

An association can persist even when the proposed treatment has no effect. Illustrative synthetic example: among 500 customers, 150 who use a budgeting app save £40 per month, while 350 non-users save £30 per month. The observed difference is £40 − £30 = £10 per month. That £10 is a group contrast, not the amount the same users would have saved without the app. Suppose app users were already saving £8 more per month before download; a simple before-treatment comparison would leave only £2 per month as a rough residual, though changing prices or habits could still matter. The comparison requires a credible design and a defined month. It does not establish causation or persistence. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Penn State STAT 507 — Bias and Confounding’ in the linked sources.

Suppose an analyst asks whether a financial-literacy email changes diversified-fund enrollment. In an illustrative synthetic audit, the email offer X and enrollment Y are recorded, but the analyst adjusts for “opened a follow-up adviser call” M. Opening that call may be caused by X (the offer prompts questions) and by an unmeasured concern U (worried customers seek advice): X → M ← U. M is therefore a collider, not a safe control. Conditioning on M can manufacture an association between the randomized offer and U, distorting the offer’s intention-to-treat estimate even though random assignment made X comparable in expectation. Use this diagnostic sequence: state the estimand (the effect of offering the email), draw arrows using pre-treatment knowledge, exclude post-offer variables such as M from the primary adjustment set, and then report any secondary analysis as assumption-dependent. If the goal instead is the effect of actually reading the email, random assignment alone does not identify it because reading is compliance-mediated; that requires additional assumptions and a different estimand. The numbers here are synthetic, and the DAG is a hypothesis to defend, not evidence of an effect.
lessons.takeaway: A causal claim needs a credible comparison for the outcome that was not observed.

practice.question: Customers who choose a low-fee fund have 2 percentage points higher annual returns than other customers. Is the 2-point difference automatically a causal effect of low fees?
practice.hint: Ask what else may influence both fund choice and returns.
practice.solution: No. Financial literacy, income, risk tolerance, account age or asset allocation may confound the association. A randomized fee intervention or a justified quasi-experiment would be needed for a causal interpretation.

lessons.title: Potential outcomes and treatment effects
lessons.body:
Let Y(1) denote a unit's outcome if treated and Y(0) its outcome without treatment. The individual effect is Y(1) − Y(0), but it cannot usually be observed directly because one person cannot occupy both conditions at once. An average treatment effect (ATE) is E[Y(1) − Y(0)] for a specified population; a sample estimate is a difference between group means when design assumptions justify it. In an illustrative randomized test, 100 treated customers show 18% enrollment and 100 controls show 12%. The estimated ATE is 18% − 12% = 6 percentage points, not a promise for every customer.

Consider a council deciding whether to offer jobseekers a travel-supported training place. For applicant i, Yᵢ(1) records whether they would be in paid work three months later if offered a place, while Yᵢ(0) records the same applicant’s outcome without the offer. The individual effect Yᵢ(1) − Yᵢ(0) is either −1, 0 or +1 for this binary outcome, but only one potential outcome is observed. A randomized offer can estimate an average effect for the eligible group; it cannot reveal both outcomes for each person. This is a constructed example, not programme data.

The individual effect Yᵢ(1) − Yᵢ(0) is either −1, 0 or +1 for this binary outcome, but only one potential outcome is observed. A randomized offer can estimate an average effect for the eligible group; it cannot reveal both outcomes for each person. This is a constructed example, not programme data. See Matheus Facure’s Chapter 02, “Randomised Experiments,” in the linked sources below.

Potential outcomes clarify why an average treatment effect is a population summary rather than a personal guarantee. Illustrative synthetic example: 80 applicants are randomly offered coaching and 80 are not. After six months, 28 offered applicants and 20 controls are employed. The offer-group rate is 28/80 = 35%, and the control rate is 20/80 = 25%, so the estimated intention-to-treat effect is 35% − 25% = 10 percentage points. Some may gain, remain unchanged, or be harmed; the group average does not reveal which person belongs to which category. Randomization supports the comparison if assignment is followed and outcomes are measured consistently. It does not reveal both potential outcomes for any applicant or guarantee this 10-point effect elsewhere. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 02: Randomised Experiments (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.

An estimand check starts by fixing the outcome scale. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose 500 eligible small firms are randomly offered a bookkeeping subsidy and 500 receive usual information; after 12 months, 75 offered firms and 100 comparison firms have entered insolvency. The risk is 75/500 = 0.150, versus 100/500 = 0.200. The intention-to-treat risk difference is 0.150 − 0.200 = −0.050, or 5 percentage points fewer insolvencies per 100 firms offered the subsidy. The risk ratio is 0.150/0.200 = 0.75: the offered group’s observed risk is 75% of the comparison risk, a 25% relative reduction. The absolute and relative statements answer different questions. With random assignment, consistent outcome measurement, and limited differential attrition, this contrast estimates the average effect of the offer for these eligible firms over 12 months. It does not show that every firm benefited, identify who would be protected in both counterfactual worlds, or establish effects outside the eligibility rules. If take-up is incomplete, calling this the effect of receiving the subsidy changes the estimand and requires further assumptions.
lessons.takeaway: Name the estimand and population; an average effect is not an effect for every person.

practice.question: In the illustrative test above, what is the estimated effect in percentage points, and what does randomization contribute?
practice.hint: Subtract the control rate from the treatment rate, then distinguish identification from precision.
practice.solution: The estimate is 6 percentage points (0.18 − 0.12). Random assignment makes treatment independent of baseline characteristics in expectation, supporting a causal comparison within the eligible population; it does not guarantee a large effect, eliminate sampling uncertainty or prove generalization.

lessons.title: Randomized experiments and implementation
lessons.body:
Random assignment balances observed and unobserved pre-treatment factors in expectation, so a treatment-control contrast can identify an intention-to-treat effect when outcomes and assignment are measured correctly. Check compliance, attrition, interference between customers and whether the treatment was delivered as planned. Suppose a message is assigned to 200 customers per arm, but only 160 treated customers actually view it. The assignment effect still answers the policy question of offering the message; it is not automatically the effect among viewers. Report the assignment rule, exclusions, missing outcomes, uncertainty interval and practical threshold. Statistical significance alone does not establish useful practical impact.

Implementation determines whether an experiment estimates an offer effect or an effect of actually receiving treatment. Synthetic example: 300 customers per arm are assigned a budgeting webinar. In the offer arm, 210 attend; enrollment is 27% among all 300 offered customers, versus 22% among 300 controls. The intention-to-treat estimate is 27% − 22% = 5 percentage points. Dividing 5 points by the 70% attendance rate gives about 7.14 points, but that is not automatically a valid treatment-on-the-treated effect: non-attenders may differ from attenders, and assignment can affect behavior even without attendance. Assume assignment is random, outcomes are recorded for all 600 customers, and contamination is limited. The result concerns offering one webinar over the stated follow-up period, not guaranteed long-run enrollment. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Matheus Facure — Ch. 02: Randomised Experiments (Causal Inference for the Brave and True; open-source handbook)’ in the linked sources.

One useful implementation choice is to prespecify a baseline outcome or prognostic score for precision, without treating adjustment as a substitute for randomization. Illustrative synthetic example: 100 customers per arm receive either an investing lesson or a neutral message. The follow-up outcome is monthly saving, measured in dollars per month; its mean is $70 in the offer arm and $64 in control, so the unadjusted intention-to-treat difference is $70 − $64 = $6 per month. Suppose a pre-specified linear ANCOVA uses a financial-literacy score measured before assignment, with baseline means 60 (offer) and 56 (control), and an estimated slope of $0.50 per score point. The illustrative adjusted contrast is $6 − $0.50 × (60 − 56) = $4 per month. This does not claim the message caused only $4: the baseline imbalance can be chance, and the slope and model are assumptions used to improve precision. Report both contrasts, uncertainty calculated for the chosen model, and the adjustment rule. Never adjust for lesson attendance or another post-assignment variable, because doing so can change the intention-to-treat estimand or induce bias.
lessons.takeaway: Randomization helps identification, while implementation and measurement determine which effect was actually estimated.

lessons.title: DAGs: confounders, mediators and colliders
lessons.body:
A directed acyclic graph (DAG) records a causal story with arrows. If financial literacy affects both message exposure and saving, it is a confounder; adjusting for it can block a non-causal backdoor path when measured before treatment. A mediator lies on the treatment-to-outcome pathway: controlling for message-induced confidence can remove part of the total effect. A collider is caused by two variables; conditioning on account approval, caused by both income and a promotional offer, can create a spurious association. Adjustment is not a checklist. Choose variables from timing and mechanism, and state what effect—total or direct—you intend to estimate.

In an illustrative apprenticeship study, prior work experience may affect both enrolment and later earnings, making it a plausible confounder. A current job type could instead sit on the pathway from training to earnings; controlling for it would remove part of the total effect. Restricting the sample to applicants who received an interview can also be risky if both training and unmeasured motivation affect interview receipt: selection on that shared consequence may create a misleading association. Draw the assumed arrows before choosing controls, and state whether the target is a total or direct effect. These pathways are hypotheses for a design, not empirical findings.

A current job type could instead sit on the pathway from training to earnings; controlling for it would remove part of the total effect. Restricting the sample to applicants who received an interview can also be risky if both training and unmeasured motivation affect interview receipt: selection on that shared consequence may create a misleading association. Draw the assumed arrows before choosing controls, and state whether the target is a total or direct effect. These pathways are hypotheses for a design, not empirical findings. See Matheus Facure’s Chapter 04, “Graphical Causal Models,” in the linked sources below.

A DAG helps distinguish a variable worth adjusting for from one that creates bias when conditioned on. Illustrative synthetic example: among customers with matched account age, 60% offered coaching open a savings account, compared with 50% not offered. If prior financial literacy raises both the chance of receiving coaching and account opening, literacy is a confounder; adjusting for it may make the comparison more credible. If coaching first increases a savings plan, that plan is a mediator, so controlling for it would remove part of the total coaching effect. If analysts keep only customers approved for a loan, and both coaching and income affect approval, approval is a collider. That 10-point gap need not be causal. These are hypothetical pathways, not observed facts; timing and measurement must support the graph. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Harvard — Causal Directed Acyclic Graphs’ in the linked sources.

Suppose, purely illustratively, that a lender wants the effect of offering a budgeting tool on on-time repayment, and prior income is the only measured pre-treatment confounder. In a synthetic dataset, 50% of eligible borrowers are in a lower-income stratum: the tool-group repayment rates are 40% (lower) and 80% (higher), while comparison rates are 30% and 75%. Standardize both groups to the same 50–50 income mix: the tool mean is 0.5(0.40) + 0.5(0.80) = 0.60, and the comparison mean is 0.5(0.30) + 0.5(0.75) = 0.525, so the standardized contrast is 0.075, or 7.5 percentage points. This calculation is preferable to a raw gap when group composition differs, but it is not automatically causal. Before labeling 7.5 percentage points an effect, check that income was measured before the offer, every stratum has support in both groups, treatment assignment is as-if random within strata (or exchangeability is otherwise credible), outcomes are defined identically, and the tool does not alter which borrowers remain observed. A post-offer repayment behavior would be a mediator, not a routine adjustment variable.
lessons.takeaway: Adjust for justified pre-treatment confounders, not automatically for every measured variable.

practice.question: A promotion affects account approval, and income also affects approval. Why can restricting analysis to approved accounts bias the promotion-return relationship?
practice.hint: Identify what kind of DAG node approval may be.
practice.solution: Approval is a collider on paths from promotion and income. Conditioning on it can open a non-causal path between promotion and income, making the groups differ in income for a design-created reason. The exact bias depends on the full data-generating process.

lessons.title: Difference-in-differences and thresholds
lessons.body:
Difference-in-differences (DiD) compares before-to-after change in a treated group with change in a comparison group. In an illustrative policy, treated firms move from 10% to 16% adoption, while controls move from 8% to 10%. The DiD estimate is (16 − 10) − (10 − 8) = 4 percentage points. Its key assumption is parallel trends: absent treatment, both groups would have changed similarly. Inspect pre-period trends, anticipate spillovers and account for staggered timing. Regression discontinuity instead compares units just above and below a cutoff; it needs no precise manipulation and continuity of potential outcomes at the threshold. Neither design becomes causal merely because its p-value is small.

Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data; weekly employment rate, measured in percentage points over two quarters): suppose a town introduces a subsidized bus pass in Quarter 2 for Northside residents, while similar Southside remains a comparison area. Northside employment is 54% in Q1 and 60% in Q2, a +6 percentage-point change. Southside is 52% and 55%, a +3-point change. Difference-in-differences = (60−54)−(55−52) = 6−3 = 3 percentage points. The estimate says Northside employment improved 3 points more than the comparison area after the subsidy, under the design assumptions. The Q2 gap is 5 points (60−55), but that is not the DiD; Northside’s own 6-point increase also includes changes shared by both areas.

Difference-in-differences can identify an average policy effect when the comparison group provides a credible counterfactual trend; it cannot by itself prove that the subsidy caused the entire post-period difference or that every resident benefited. The key check is parallel trends: inspect several pre-policy quarters and plot both areas, looking for similar movements before Q2; a placebo policy date can provide an additional diagnostic. Watch for spillovers, such as Southside residents using the passes, or different employment measurement across areas. A common mistake is to call Northside’s 6-point before-to-after rise the treatment effect, ignoring the comparison change. See “World Bank DIME — Causal Inference and Quasi-Experimental Methods” in the linked sources below.

A threshold design identifies a local comparison, not automatically a policy effect for everyone. Illustrative synthetic example: a grant is offered to firms scoring at least 70 on an eligibility index. Firms just below the cutoff have a 52% three-month adoption rate, while firms just above have 59%; the jump is 59% − 52% = 7 percentage points. Because the groups are close to 70, the comparison can be credible if firms cannot precisely manipulate scores and other determinants change smoothly at the cutoff. The 7-point estimate applies near score 70, for this grant and three-month period; it need not apply to firms scoring 40 or 95. A small sample or a narrow score window can also make the estimate imprecise. For a fuller treatment, see ‘World Bank DIME — Causal Inference and Quasi-Experimental Methods’ in the linked sources.

With staggered adoption, calculate cohort-specific contrasts before pooling them. Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data): Region A adopts a training subsidy in Q2; its monthly earnings rise from $2,000 in Q1 to $2,120 in Q2, while a not-yet-treated comparison rises from $1,800 to $1,880. A's DiD is ($120 − $80) = $40 per worker-month. Region B adopts in Q3; from Q2 to Q3 its earnings rise from $1,500 to $1,590, while the comparison rises from $1,880 to $1,950, giving ($90 − $70) = $20 per worker-month. If the estimand is the equal-weight average across these two adoption cohorts, it is ($40 + $20)/2 = $30 per worker-month—not the difference between the final regional levels. This calculation requires parallel trends separately in each comparison window, no anticipation before adoption, no spillovers into the comparison, and consistent earnings measurement. A pooled regression that treats already-subsidized regions as controls for later adopters can mix treatment effects into the counterfactual; define the cohort and time weights explicitly. The result remains an average for these cohorts and windows, not automatically an effect for regions that adopt earlier, later, or never.
lessons.takeaway: Quasi-experimental credibility comes from explicit, testable design assumptions, not from the label or sample size.

practice.question: Using the adoption rates above, calculate the DiD estimate and state its central identifying assumption.
practice.solution: Treatment change is 6 points; control change is 2 points; their difference is 4 percentage points. The central assumption is that, without the policy, the treated group would have followed the control group's change on average (parallel trends), subject to no problematic spillovers or simultaneous shocks.

lessons.title: Instrumental variables, uncertainty and transport
lessons.body:
An instrumental variable (IV) changes treatment but affects the outcome only through that treatment. A credible IV requires relevance, an exclusion restriction and an appropriate independence story; these are substantive assumptions, not outputs of a regression. In a toy example, an encouragement raises fund adoption by 0.50 (50 percentage points) and raises average saving by 0.02 dollars per dollar of income, so the Wald estimate is 0.02 ÷ 0.50 = 0.04, or 4 cents per dollar for compliers under the design. Report uncertainty, first-stage strength, treatment version, target population and limits on transport. A causal estimate can be internally credible yet practically small or externally narrow.

An instrumental variable can estimate an effect for compliers when its assumptions are plausible, but the arithmetic and target must be stated carefully. Illustrative synthetic example: an encouragement is randomly sent to 200 customers; 40 adopt a savings plan, versus 20 of 200 not encouraged. Adoption rises 40/200 − 20/200 = 20% − 10% = 10 percentage points. Average monthly deposits rise from £18 to £20, a difference of £2 per month. The Wald estimate is £2 ÷ 0.10 = £20 per month per full-unit adoption effect, interpreted for compliers under the model. This requires relevance, independence, and no direct effect of encouragement on deposits except through adoption. It does not prove a £20 increase for every customer or transport to another product, month, or population. For a fuller treatment, see ‘World Bank DIME — Causal Inference and Quasi-Experimental Methods’ in the linked sources.

Use the Wald ratio by keeping the two intention-to-treat effects in their native units. Illustrative synthetic example: among 400 eligible borrowers, a randomly assigned reminder produces repayment-plan enrollment for 160 people (40%) versus 100 (25%) under no reminder, so the first stage is 0.40 − 0.25 = 0.15, or 15 percentage points. Suppose mean annual interest paid is $108 in the reminder group and $112.50 in the control group; the reduced form is $108 − $112.50 = −$4.50 per borrower-year. Dividing gives −$4.50 ÷ 0.15 = −$30 per borrower-year per one-unit increase in enrollment: under the IV assumptions, compliers who enroll because of the reminder pay $30 less annual interest on average. The negative sign indicates lower interest, not a loss. This is not $30 for every borrower: always-enrollers and never-enrollers are not identified by this instrument. The interpretation also requires no direct reminder effect on interest, no spillovers, and a sufficiently strong first stage; report an interval because sampling error in both stages can make a ratio unstable.
lessons.takeaway: Identification assumptions determine what a design can claim; uncertainty and scope determine how useful that claim is.

caseStudy: Consider an educational brokerage experiment using deliberately illustrative, simulated numbers. Eligible customers are randomly offered either a low-cost index-fund education message or a neutral message. After three months, 18% of 200 offered customers enroll in a diversified fund, compared with 12% of 200 controls: the intention-to-treat difference is 6 percentage points. Before interpreting it, check that assignment was concealed, exposure was recorded, outcomes were measured consistently, attrition was balanced and customers could not contaminate one another. The estimate answers the effect of offering this message to this eligible population during this period; it does not estimate a universal effect or fund performance. A voluntary-choice comparison would be confounded by literacy, income, risk tolerance and account age. A small p-value would not prove the message caused enrollment, establish financial benefit or make the effect practically important. Pre-specify a meaningful enrollment threshold, report an interval, disclose deviations and consider whether behavior persists. This is a teaching example, not investment advice.
misconceptions: A significant regression coefficient proves causation. Identification comes from design and assumptions, not the p-value.
Adjusting for every available variable always removes bias. Mediators, colliders and post-treatment variables can introduce bias.
More data solve systematic confounding. Sample size reduces some noise, not structural bias.
Random assignment guarantees perfect balance and universal generalization. Balance is probabilistic, and transport depends on the population, treatment and context.
A non-significant result proves no effect, while a significant result proves a useful effect. Precision, effect size, practical thresholds and design credibility must be assessed separately.

quiz.question: Why does random assignment help estimate a treatment effect?
options: It guarantees every participant has the same outcome.
It tends to make treatment groups comparable on baseline factors in expectation.
It proves the result generalizes to every population.
quiz.explanation: Random assignment supports causal identification within the study. Generalization still depends on the sampling frame and context.
